title: The cheerful reply to an angry customer
scenario:
You lead a small support team at an online furniture shop. The team uses an AI assistant to draft replies to customer reviews. To set the tone, a teammate added three example replies to the prompt. Most drafts are now great. But last week a customer wrote that her sofa arrived broken, and the draft began: "Thank you so much for your lovely feedback!"

The exhibit shows the examples in the prompt.
exhibit:
Write a reply to the customer review below. Match the style of the examples.

<examples>
Review: "Love the oak table, fast delivery!"
Reply: Thank you so much for your lovely feedback, Ana! Enjoy the table. - Sam, Support

Review: "Great chair, very comfy."
Reply: Thank you so much for your lovely feedback, Tom! Happy sitting. - Sam, Support

Review: "Beautiful lamp, five stars."
Reply: Thank you so much for your lovely feedback, Lea! Enjoy the light. - Sam, Support
</examples>

Review: [new review here]

questions.prompt: Why did the draft thank the customer for a complaint?

options.text: All three examples are happy reviews with the same opening, so the model learned that pattern.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's guide warns that examples which don't vary enough can teach unintended patterns. Here the pattern was: always open by thanking the customer for lovely feedback.

options.text: The model can't detect that a review is negative, so it treats every review the same way.
options.explanation: Nothing suggests the model can't read a complaint. The examples showed only one opening for every review, so it used that opening.

options.text: The examples were wrapped in tags, and tags make the model copy the text word for word.
options.explanation: Tags only help the model tell examples apart from the task. The problem is what the examples contain, not the tags.

options.text: Three examples are too few for a model to learn any tone, so it fell back to a default reply.
options.explanation: Anthropic's guide suggests 3–5 examples. Three was enough for the model to learn a pattern. It learned the wrong one.

options.text: Add a line at the top: "Be careful with negative reviews."
options.explanation: This helps a little, but the examples still show only one kind of reply. The model still has no example of how a good complaint reply looks.

options.text: Replace one happy example with a real reply to a complaint, written in the same format.
options.explanation: Right. Varied examples cover the cases you actually get, and the same format keeps the signal clear. The guides from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google all ask for varied examples.

options.text: Remove all the examples and describe the tone in one long paragraph of instructions instead.
options.explanation: The examples gave you the tone and length you liked. Gemini's guide recommends always including examples. Fix them instead of dropping them.

options.text: Keep the examples but tell the model to write each reply in a different style from them.
options.explanation: Then the model loses the tone the team wanted. The examples should show good replies for each kind of review.

questions.prompt: A teammate says: "Let's paste all 200 of our past replies as examples. More is better." What do you answer?

options.text: Yes. With 200 replies the model learns more, so it will stop making mistakes like this one.
options.explanation: No number of examples removes mistakes. And the guides do not say more is always better.

options.text: Yes, but only use the replies to happy customers, since those have the tone we want.
options.explanation: That repeats the problem you just found: no variety, so the model learns one pattern.

options.text: No. Too many examples can make the model copy them too closely. Pick 3–5 varied ones.
options.explanation: Right. Gemini's guide warns that with too many examples the model may overfit. More examples also make each prompt longer.

options.text: No. Models can only read a single example at a time, so the rest would be ignored.
options.explanation: Models can read many examples. The issue is overfitting and cost, not a limit of one.

questions.prompt: The examples use real customer first names (Ana, Tom, Lea). The prompt will be shared across the whole team. What should you do?

options.text: Keep the names. Real customer data makes the examples more relevant and more natural.
options.explanation: Relevant means the same kind of task, not real personal data. A shared prompt spreads those names to everyone who uses it.

options.text: Replace the names with made-up ones, and check for order numbers or emails too.
options.explanation: Right. The example still teaches the pattern, and no real customer's details are copied into a shared prompt.

options.text: Delete the names and leave the gap empty, like "Thank you, !", so no data is shared.
options.explanation: An empty gap is a pattern too. The model may copy the broken greeting into real replies.

options.text: Ask the model to forget the names after each reply it writes, so nothing is kept.
options.explanation: The names are part of the prompt itself, so they are sent with every request. Remove them from the prompt.
